reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: Episodic, reversible digital vasospasm provoked by cold or emotional stress, classically producing a triphasic colour change of pallor, then cyanosis, then reactive hyperaemia
Primary Raynaud is common, typically begins in young women, is symmetric, and occurs without an underlying disease or tissue damage
Secondary Raynaud arises from an underlying condition, most importantly connective tissue disease, and carries a greater risk of digital ischaemia and ulceration
Features favouring a secondary cause include older age at onset, asymmetry, digital ulcers or pitting scars, and abnormal nailfold capillaries
A positive antinuclear antibody and abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy suggest an evolving connective tissue disease, often systemic sclerosis
General measures emphasise cold avoidance, keeping the whole body warm, and smoking cessation
Pharmacological therapy, when needed, uses vasodilators (calcium channel blockers first-line, with other agents for refractory or ischaemic disease)
Critical digital ischaemia is an emergency requiring urgent assessment and consideration of secondary causes
reference.pathophysiology: Raynaud phenomenon results from exaggerated vasoconstriction of digital arteries, precapillary arterioles, and cutaneous arteriovenous shunts in response to cold or stress. In primary disease this reflects a functional imbalance of vascular tone with heightened sympathetic and local vascular reactivity and no structural vessel damage. In secondary disease, structural vasculopathy, endothelial dysfunction, and abnormal balance of vasoconstrictors (such as endothelin) and vasodilators (such as nitric oxide), often in the setting of systemic sclerosis or other connective tissue disease, produce fixed narrowing that predisposes to persistent ischaemia, ulceration, and tissue loss.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic sclerosis and other connective tissue diseases (secondary Raynaud)
Thoracic outlet syndrome and other causes of arterial compression
Atherosclerotic or embolic peripheral arterial disease
Vibration-induced (hand-arm) vascular injury and occupational causes
additionalInvestigations: Nailfold capillaroscopy to distinguish primary from secondary disease
Antinuclear antibody and, if positive, connective tissue disease-specific antibodies
Inflammatory markers and assessment for features of systemic autoimmune disease
Vascular assessment for fixed arterial obstruction when ischaemia is asymmetric or severe
Targeted investigations for occupational, drug, or haematological causes when suspected
redFlags: Digital ulceration, gangrene, or critical ischaemia threatening tissue loss
Asymmetric or unilateral symptoms suggesting fixed arterial obstruction or embolism
New Raynaud phenomenon in an older adult indicating a likely secondary cause
Accompanying features of connective tissue disease such as skin tightening, dysphagia, or breathlessness
Abnormal nailfold capillaries with positive autoantibodies signalling evolving systemic sclerosis
reference.prognosis: Primary Raynaud phenomenon is benign, usually stable or improving over time, and rarely causes tissue damage. Secondary Raynaud has a more variable outlook determined by the underlying disease and carries a real risk of digital ulceration and loss, particularly in systemic sclerosis.
pitfalls: Labelling all Raynaud as benign primary disease without screening for secondary causes
Missing evolving systemic sclerosis by not performing nailfold capillaroscopy and autoantibody testing
Underestimating critical digital ischaemia as ordinary vasospasm
Overlooking drug, occupational, or vascular contributors
Neglecting non-pharmacological measures such as whole-body warming and smoking cessation
management: General measures of whole-body warming, cold avoidance, smoking cessation and withdrawal of vasoconstrictive drugs
First-line dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine to reduce attack frequency and severity
Second-line vasodilators including phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, topical nitrates or angiotensin-receptor blockers when calcium-channel blockers are insufficient
Intravenous prostacyclin analogues such as iloprost for critical digital ischaemia, and endothelin-receptor antagonists such as bosentan to prevent recurrent digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis
Identification and treatment of an underlying connective tissue disease in secondary disease, guided by antinuclear antibody testing and nailfold capillaroscopy
Surveillance for digital ulceration and tissue loss, with rheumatology referral when a secondary cause is suspected
Management of a digital ischaemic crisis with prostanoids and consideration of botulinum toxin or digital sympathectomy
